messages.subject: [R-S] S/R neutral
messages.body_plain:
>I think it would be very useful to have one or more documents
>clearly describing the differences and techniques for writing
>implementation-neutral S code. For instance, a document, say a HOWTO,
>describing techniques for ...

Before writing documentation I think it would be good to work out a
reasonable common strategy for supporting "neutral" code. After several
years of making my S (Splus 3.3) code work also in R I have just
converted to making my R code work also in S. I did this conversion
mainly because of the package support in R. The mechanisms for checking
documentation and running tests are very useful. In S I mimic R by using
some scripts to run tests in the tests directory, but I have not tried
to integrate the help with any newer Splus help systems.

I find making "R code work also in Splus" to be much cleaner in several
respects than making "Splus code work also in R." I think this is
because it seems reasonable to tell R users to upgrade, while backwards
compatability is more of an issue in Splus (perhaps especially for me
since I have not converted to using the newer classes and methods in S).

There are many more detailed issues, but I think everyone could benefit
from a common general strategy, so perhaps we could try to work that out
first.

Paul Gilbert

messages.subject: [R-S] The SLanguage package
messages.body_plain:
This package, part of the Omegahat software, is a first cut at
providing tools to help write compatible S language software.

What exists currently are R and S-plus versions of a package/library
with some functions designed to smooth over a few of the
inconsistencies (e.g., different argument names) and patch a few holes
(facilities defined in one implementation but not in the other).

The versions currently available are definitely early, trying to
suggest that this is a useful exercise but not at all implying any
final decisions.  An overview and tar archives are available at
  http://www.omegahat.org/SLanguage/

The web documentation says a little about the underlying strategy.

Several areas are in process but not yet included:

-  C programming tools (e.g., header files) to bridge some of the
   incompatibilities at the C level.

-  documentation tools.  Mainly this will use the work on XML-based
   documentation going on in parallel.

-  tools for organizing compatible packages.  This will help
   programmers get started with their own packages, such that they can
   maintain compatible source and generate copies of their package for
   both S-Plus and R.  

The material now available is too incomplete to recommend to general
users, but readers of r-sig-s might find it worth looking at.  In any
case, comments and suggestions are very much needed.

John

messages.subject: [R-S] The SLanguage package
messages.body_plain:
John

I have never had very good luck redefining functions in order to resolve
inconsistencies between various versions of R and S, as you do in
SLanguage (e.g. get, exists).  First, it is difficult to tests all the
variants on all the different platforms to make sure something has not
been broken, and second, future versions always have a habit of changing
something which makes maintenance very difficult. Instead, it seems
better to define a new function which has a consistent behaviour.

For example, unlink() has a different behaviour with directories in
different versions of Splus. R has added the argument recursive=FALSE.
It is possible to redefine unlink in Splus to support the recursive
argument, but the default behaviour will then be changed in some
versions of Splus and something is certain to break. Instead, it seems
better to defined a new function (maybe SRunlink) which has a consistent
behaviour and can be use instead of unlink in other code.

This implies that users of these tools will be designing their code to
run in both S and R, rather than simply porting in the simplest possible
manner, but in the end I think this distinction will be necessary
anyway.

Paul Gilbert

I sympathize, but on the other hand we should try to do as much as
possible to make _most_ cases work easily for the programmer.

The bottom line is that we don't want just a few, super-industrious
people to write compatible code.  Yes, for sure there are aspects that
CAN'T be handled without the programmer worrying explicitly about
compatibility.

When we get to very basic stuff, however, it seems worth trying to
make things as easy as possible.

Before requiring programmers to use, say, Sget instead of get within
their code, let's see if we can't at least go nearly all the way with
a version of get itself.  It may turn out that some examples DO
require a special function, but allowing those examples to force
programmers to change all their code is likely to discourage
participation.

Agreed that this is likely to require more work initially (I just had
to revise the get function today to match R usage more accurately),
but if it reduces frustration for larger groups of programmers, it
should be worth it.

Anyway, the SLanguage package is there for people to play with and, I
hope, add to.  Let's try a variety of approaches and see what works.
 
By the way, a terminology suggestion: I've tried to use the letter "S"
by itself to mean something defined for the S language, both R and
S-Plus.  So I would call the new `unlink' function `Sunlink' (if
nobody has gotten to that name before), if we needed one.

John

messages.subject: [R-S] The SLanguage package
messages.body_plain:
John

>I sympathize, but on the other hand we should try to do as much as
>possible to make _most_ cases work easily for the programmer.

Having spent a great deal of time tracking down cases that don't work,
I'm not so sure that this is a good idea. I like to use functions that
are defined with a consistent behaviour in mind and are intended to work
the same way all of the time, not just most of the time.  I realize that
this is not exactly what you meant to say, but R and S are already
fairly compatible at a superficial level so I do not think the audience
for a package like SLanguage will be casual users, and programmers will
not want to use it if it breaks things that usually work. For most users
it is already easy to write compatible code. (It is mainly a question of
knowing a few things to avoid.)

>Yes, for sure there are aspects that CAN'T be handled without the
>programmer worrying explicitly about compatibility.

I think there may be two levels of compatibility to worry about. As you
point out, things get rather more complicated if one tries to program
using environments and language objects. Looking at SLanguage I see that
most of the things you are working on are things that have not been an
issue for me, mainly because I have avoided them. Perhaps there is a
natural way to split this into different pieces.

What I am thinking about is a much more simplistic level, where
compatibility should not be an issue but it is. At this level many of
the problems have to do with the operating system interface rather than
R/S language differences. Most of these problems are handled just by
using the R function names and defining functions for S (e.g. Platform,
Sys.info, Sys.sleep, getwd). In part it is easier to use the R
definitions in S because backwards compatibility has not been an issue
in R, and these functions have consistent cross platform definitions. In
part it is simpler because the names have not been used in S so S/R
differences are less of an issue. One case (perhaps the only one) where
this does not work is for unlink.

>(I just had to revise the get function today to match R usage more
>accurately)

Yes, the version I downloaded this morning causes problems in my code.
Also, the DESCRIPTION file had some errors (it looked like the package
name and version were suppose to be automatically filled in, but
weren't) and when you get test code it needs to be in SLanguage/tests
not SLanguage/inst/tests or "R CMD check" will not run it.

Paul Gilbert
